First verify the working conditions and authority: this occupation carries passengers per routes, shifts, and safety procedures and does not change approved routes, stops, or fares on its own, nor does it replace the operating enterprise's production safety responsibility. If the target position's vehicle class, practice qualification, health, and institutional training requirements have not been verified, pause high-cost investment first; being able to drive a car, having a mentor, or holding a single certificate does not automatically permit commercial passenger driving.

Low-cost experience: use only pen and paper to complete the fictional shift in T1 below, calculating a planned 27 minutes, 12 kilometers, 15 yuan receivable, and cash 1 yuan short; write out the vehicle warning to be verified, the unknown actual time, and a draft report. Keep the calculation and the revision, and check against the reference deliverable; a paper result only supports continuing to learn. Ride-along observation or practical training must be arranged by a lawful institution per the rules, and you must not drive or carry passengers yourself.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to verify the vehicle, route, fares, and log per the timetable and procedures, and still accept review and correction when facing passenger problems and time pressure. First observe whether you mark unknown states in the T1 paper exercise and explain the difference without guessing responsibility; a correct calculation is not a driving competence conclusion, and actual employment still requires lawful qualifications, health conditions, and employer assessment authorization.

Education, qualifications, and authorization must be verified separately: O*NET lists this occupation's preparation level as Job Zone 1-2 (SVP below 6.0), usually requiring a high school diploma or equivalent or GED, with on-the-job training from a few days to a year; in the United States, bus drivers usually need a commercial driver's license (CDL) and must meet driving record, medical examination, and vision and hearing requirements, and some positions may require a background check; in mainland China, drivers engaged in commercial road passenger transport must hold the corresponding motor vehicle driving license for more than 1 year, be no older than 63, have no major or greater at-fault traffic accident within 3 years, master road passenger transport regulations and basic passenger first aid knowledge, and pass an examination to obtain the corresponding practice qualification certificate (Provisions on the Administration of Road Transport Practitioners); urban public bus and trolleybus drivers must also hold a motor vehicle driving license matching the vehicle class with the internship period completed, and have no violation record of 12 points or more in the most recent 3 consecutive scoring cycles, among others (Provisions on the Administration of Urban Public Bus and Trolleybus Passenger Transport).

One sentence: this is a position centered on safe driving, passenger transport service, vehicle inspection, and operating records, and its outputs are reviewable driving and fare records, transport service completed per schedule, and anomaly information reported and escalated per procedures; it is not a role that decides routes and fares on its own, nor does it replace the operating unit's production safety responsibility. The work of this occupation can be divided into three categories: first, safe driving and operations (driving per the schedule and approved route, stopping properly, obeying traffic laws, adjusting to weather and road conditions, and ensuring passengers ride smoothly and safely); second, passenger service and ticketing (announcing routes and stops, assisting elderly or disabled passengers and others, collecting tickets and fares, reminding passengers to maintain order, answering questions about schedules and routes, and handling passenger emergencies or service disruptions); third, vehicle inspection and record handover (inspecting the vehicle and fuel, oil, and water levels before departure, keeping the vehicle clean, recording fares and driving information and maintaining the log, reporting delays and accidents, and completing end-of-shift and fare and vehicle condition handover). All three share the same work chain centered on safe driving and reviewable records.
Safe driving and operations

Depart per the schedule and approved route → stop properly at stops and load and unload passengers → obey traffic laws and drive smoothly → adjust speed and following distance to road and weather conditions → ensure passengers ride smoothly and safely → complete handover per the shift requirements on arrival.
Passenger service and ticketing

Announce routes and stops → assist elderly or disabled passengers and others in boarding and alighting → answer questions about schedules and routes → collect tickets or cash fares and apply the fare rules → remind passengers to be seated and maintain order in the cabin → handle passenger emergencies or service disruptions and report promptly.

Inspect the vehicle before departure and check gasoline, oil, and water levels, record fares and driving information per shift and maintain the log, keep the vehicle clean, report delays or accidents per procedures, and complete end-of-shift handover of fares and vehicle condition.

Intercity and urban transit bus drivers produce passenger transport completed per schedule; school bus drivers address student commuting with different requirements for minor supervision and school procedures; shuttle and limousine drivers address hotel, airport, and corporate transfers with different service objects and shift patterns; taxi drivers operate on meter per passenger instructions, generally not on fixed routes and schedules; rail locomotive drivers and subway and tram drivers work on fixed rail systems with different qualifications and signal rules; baggage porters and bellhops mainly handle baggage and traveler assistance, and some positions also provide transfers or arrange transport, so they cannot all be called non-driving. Similar names or working in the same transport industry do not mean qualifications, responsibility boundaries, and operating models are interchangeable.
Core purpose

Deliver passengers safely, punctually, and smoothly per the schedule and approved route, obey traffic laws and operating service specifications, keep cabin order and operating records traceable, and be responsible for driving safety and fare accuracy.
Main objects and basis

The objects are transit buses and long-distance coaches and their passengers, routes, stops, and shift arrangements; the basis is road traffic safety law and vehicle class requirements, the operating unit's driving work plans and service specifications, vehicle inspection and driving record systems, and fare and concessionary travel rules (in mainland China also the Regulations on Road Transport of the People's Republic of China, the Provisions on the Administration of Road Transport Practitioners, the Provisions on the Administration of Road Passenger Transport and Passenger Stations, and the Provisions on the Administration of Urban Public Bus and Trolleybus Passenger Transport).
Core process

Pre-departure inspection and preparation, driving and stopping per the schedule and route, stop announcements and passenger service, ticket and fare collection, anomaly and emergency handling, records and reporting, and end-of-shift handover of fares and vehicle.
Main outputs

Transport service completed per schedule, complete and reviewable driving logs and fare records, delay and accident report records, vehicle inspection and cleaning results, and end-of-shift and handover documents completed per procedures.
Responsible parties

Driving safety and passenger service are the driver's responsibility; shift scheduling and route and stop adjustments are decided by the operating unit and the competent department; the primary responsibility for production safety is borne by the operating enterprise; reporting and handling of accidents, violations, and passenger complaints follow institutional rules and applicable provisions; judgments beyond your own duties and authorization must be escalated per procedures.
Authority and approval

Changes to ordinary routes, stops, and time periods follow operating management procedures; Article 22 of the 2024 urban regulation has emergency and safety exceptions, and Article 34 permits suspending the relevant operation when unsafe. Drivers follow current emergency procedures to protect passengers promptly, handle the situation, and report, and Article 29 of the 2017 rules prohibits abandoning the vehicle and fleeing before the passengers; emergency protection should not be delayed to await approval for an ordinary change.
Conclusion boundary

The driving log and fare records state "what transport this shift completed per plan and what anomalies occurred"; they do not equal a determination of accident responsibility, nor do they replace the operating unit's safety management judgment and the competent department's regulatory conclusions, and they will change with review and subsequent handling.

Before onboarding, verify at least six items: the position basis and form of employment (bus enterprise, road passenger transport enterprise, charter or tourist transport, or outsourcing), shift and schedule arrangements (including early and last shifts and holidays), vehicle class and practice qualification requirements, fixed or rotating route and vehicle model arrangements, safety and occupational health protection arrangements (including emergency handling procedures), and the real pay method (hours, shift allowances, and performance basis).
Occupational basis

The 2022 Classification Code of Occupations, 4-02-02-01 passenger vehicle driver, includes bus drivers and urban public bus and trolleybus drivers, and also taxi and ride-hailing drivers, a scope broader than U.S. 53-3052. 4-02-02-03 road passenger transport attendant handles ticket sales and inspection and on-board service and is not a synonymous detailed class for drivers; verify against actual tasks. O*NET2025 industries: government 59%, transportation and warehousing 37%, other 4%; this is the occupational industry distribution, not wages or the Chinese bus unit industry. The OOH separately details local government (excluding education and hospitals) 54%, urban transit 17%, charter 8%, intercity and rural 5%, and other passenger transport 3%, which cannot be forcibly merged. The same BLS OOH page contains the parent summary and this occupation's detailed table, interpreted by each section's coverage.
Education and training pathway

O*NET new-entrant education Q&A: 84% high school or equivalent, 13% less than high school, and 2% postsecondary certificate, which is not the composition of current practitioners. JobZone1—2/SVP below 6 with a few days to one year is a preparation range summary; the BLS typical entry for this occupation is a high school diploma / None related experience / medium-term on-the-job training. U.S. bus drivers need a CDL and the applicable P passenger endorsement, issued by the state, verified by vehicle class and state rules; entry-level A/B or initial P, among others, require separate verification of ELDT applicability and exceptions.
Methods and tools

The detailed profile lists 3 software categories: browsers, map creation (MapQuest/MapPoint), and operating systems; the Hot list is 1 specific product, Windows, with hiring mention percentages NA (not 0). Category counts, product counts, hiring mentions, and AI deployment rates are interpreted separately.
Safety and work permits

Work risks mainly involve long periods of sitting and repetitive motion, an enclosed cabin and noise, outdoor exposure in all kinds of weather, contact with emotionally agitated passengers, exposure to disease or infection, and the consequences of traffic accidents and emergencies; O*NET work context shows 87% sit continuously or almost continuously, 82% use their hands to handle objects and tools continuously or almost continuously, 85% work inside an enclosed vehicle every day, 74% are in constant contact with others, 64% face time pressure every day, 61% say the consequences of error are extremely serious, and 83% are on a regular schedule; pre-departure inspections should be completed per procedures, driving should follow vehicle class and practice qualification requirements, emergencies should be handled per institutional procedures, and protection and emergency equipment should be used as the position requires.
Training and regulatory requirements

In China, drivers engaged in commercial road passenger transport follow Article 9 of the 2026 practice provisions: the corresponding motor vehicle driving license for at least 1 year, age no older than 63, no major or greater at-fault traffic accident within 3 years, mastery of road passenger transport regulations and basic motor vehicle repair and passenger first aid knowledge, and passing an examination to obtain the corresponding practice qualification. 63 is not the age threshold for all motor vehicle driving licenses, and urban bus positions are verified separately under urban rules. Urban buses are verified under Articles 31—32 of the 2024 regulation and Articles 27—28 of the 2017 rules for duty capability, health, no violent crime or drug record, a matching driving license with the driving probationary period completed, no full 12 points in 3 consecutive scoring cycles, and no traffic accident crime, dangerous driving crime, or drink-driving record; training and assessment must be passed before taking up the post, archives must be kept for inspection, and filing with the competent department is made per the rules.
Pay and working hours

Positions are arranged by route and shift. O*NET shows 83% on a regular schedule and 29% working more than 40 hours per week; BLS notes that early and late shifts and weekends may be included. When comparing opportunities, verify the contract pay method, overtime and allowances, and training costs separately, and do not present one pay method as a uniform industry standard.

Intercity and urban transit bus drivers (U.S. side O*NET-SOC 53-3052.00, Bus Drivers, Transit and Intercity) drive transit buses or long-distance coaches, including regular route operation, charter, and private transport; the official description includes possibly assisting passengers with baggage and possibly collecting tickets or fares. Daily work includes: driving the vehicle along a specified route or to a specified destination per the schedule and obeying traffic laws, ensuring a smooth and safe trip for passengers; stopping in the loading area to let passengers board and alight and announcing stops to passengers; inspecting the vehicle before departure and checking gasoline, oil, and water levels; assisting elderly or disabled passengers and others in boarding and alighting, confirming they are seated, helping with baggage, and answering questions about schedules and routes; collecting tickets or cash fares from passengers; handling passenger emergencies or service disruptions; reporting delays or accidents; reminding passengers to be seated and keeping order; adjusting heating, lighting, and ventilation systems for passenger comfort; recording cash and ticket revenue and other information and maintaining the driving log; keeping the vehicle clean; reading maps to plan routes; and loading and unloading baggage in the baggage compartment. It bears driving safety and passenger service responsibility, but does not replace the operating unit's production safety responsibility, nor may it decide routes, stops, and fares on its own.

Of the 14 tasks, 12 are Core and 2 Supplemental, with a further 41 general activities, 16 detailed activities, and 57 context items. The original task importance ratings and context percentages are retained; the U.S. group description is not Chinese procedures or each person's complete work list.

paragraphs: This page compares intercity and urban transit bus drivers with six adjacent occupations on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference better suits. Adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupation descriptions, and do not mean trade names are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career directions and core outputs are based on the official descriptions of O*NET 53-3052.00 and the adjacent entries (U.S. basis); the vehicle class, practice qualifications, and safety requirements of adjacent trades must be verified separately under their own jurisdictions, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut to a career change.

The table below compares the directional differences between intercity and urban transit bus drivers and adjacent trades; the basis for judgment is the main outputs, the parties responsible to, and the qualifications required, rather than the similarity of trade names.

School bus drivers address minors and require additional student supervision and school procedure requirements; this occupation addresses ordinary passengers in transit and intercity transport, with different shift and route patterns.

If you prefer working with primary and secondary school students and following the school calendar, examine school bus drivers first; if you prefer running regular transit or intercity routes, examine this occupation first.
Transport students to and from school and ensure student safety on board, with outputs mainly pickup and drop-off service completed per the school calendar and riding order records.
Bus Drivers, School
School bus monitors do not drive the vehicle and focus on student supervision and order; this occupation centers on driving and passenger service and bears driving safety responsibility.
If you prefer care and order management without driving responsibility, examine school bus monitors first; if you prefer driving a commercial bus, examine this occupation first.
Supervise students on board, assist with boarding and alighting, and maintain order, with outputs mainly safe student escort and order maintenance.
School Bus Monitors

Baggage porters and bellhops have baggage handling and traveler assistance as their main outputs; O*NET also lists transfer or transport arrangement tasks, so they cannot be summarized as never driving. The core of this occupation is providing passenger transport driving service by route and shift.
If you prefer service and carrying work and accept physical load, examine baggage porters and bellhops first; if you prefer driving a vehicle in operation, examine this occupation first.
Carry baggage at stations and hotels, assist travelers, and relay information, with outputs mainly baggage handling and traveler assistance.
Baggage Porters and Bellhops

Reservation and ticket agents handle ticketing and information at a fixed post and do not bear vehicle operation and driving safety; this occupation handles driving, fares, and passenger service on the operational frontline at the same time.

If you prefer ticketing and advisory work, examine reservation and transportation ticket agents and travel clerks first; if you prefer driving on the frontline and serving passengers directly, examine this occupation first.
Handle bookings, ticket issuance, and travel inquiries at a window or online, with outputs mainly ticketing and traveler information records.
Reservation and Transportation Ticket Agents and Travel Clerks

Dispatchers mainly arrange personnel, equipment, or vehicles and coordinate operations and anomalies; this does not equal an individual independently holding route approval authority. This occupation mainly performs passenger transport driving and bears the corresponding safety and service duties.
If you prefer operational coordination and dispatch decisions, examine dispatchers first; if you prefer driving and serving on the operational frontline, examine this occupation first.
Arrange and adjust shifts, monitor operating status, and coordinate anomaly handling, with outputs mainly dispatch instructions and operating records.
Dispatchers, Except Police, Fire, and Ambulance

Transit and railroad police have enforcement duties and corresponding qualification requirements and do not perform passenger driving tasks; this occupation centers on driving and passenger service and reports and refers violations and safety incidents per procedures.
If you prefer enforcement and safety patrol work, examine transit and railroad police first; if you prefer driving a commercial bus and providing passenger service, examine this occupation first.
Enforce the law, patrol, and handle safety incidents within the transport system, with outputs mainly enforcement and safety incident handling records.
Transit and Railroad Police

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the main outputs, the parties responsible to, and the qualifications required, not how similar the names are; once the direction is set, you should verify item by item the target position's vehicle class and practice qualification requirements, shift and schedule arrangements, route and vehicle model scope, and training and certification arrangements, and keep written confirmation.

Education and development

Focus training on safe and defensive driving, route and schedule execution, passenger service and communication, emergencies and emergency evacuation, and ticketing and driving record standards, while also training the awareness of verifying system prompts and monitoring data and the habit of proactively reporting doubtful points.

This page lists dispatch queries, stop announcements, ticketing, and records as explorable tool-assisted steps, which is an editorial suggestion organized by task, not a measured efficiency or adoption rate. The materials examined are not enough to judge this occupation's overall replacement probability or year; current lawful operation must still comply with driving qualifications, passenger safety, and reporting obligations.

values: Fictional shift and inputs

Paper shift T1: stop A 08:00 → stop B 08:12 → stop C 08:27; A—B is 5 kilometers and B—C is 7 kilometers. A flat fare of 2 yuan and a student half fare of 1 yuan: 6 full-fare passengers and 3 student passengers; electronic payment 10 yuan, cash receivable 5 yuan, and cash box actually counted at 4 yuan. The passenger concession statuses are only as given and do not correspond to a real fare system.

07:55 inspection record: lighting verification completed, on-board warning pending verification; the fictional procedure requires that all pending items be confirmed by the designated reviewer before the vehicle may be marked ready to depart. The actual departure and arrival times are not given. Log columns: planned/actual times, mileage, electronic payment, cash receivable/actually received, pending items, reporting recipient, and confirmation status; pen and paper only throughout.
Three paper tasks

Calculate the planned total time, mileage, and fares receivable in stop order; distinguish electronic payment, cash receivable, and cash actually received, write out the cash difference, and do not directly judge the difference as unlawful.

Fill in the pending items and draft report per the fictional procedure, explaining whether the vehicle can be marked ready to depart and whether the actual arrival can be determined. Use 30 minutes to read the materials and 60 minutes to fill in and recalculate; do not add a confirmation person, a repair conclusion, or an actual time on your own.
Reference deliverable and review

The planned intervals are 12 minutes and 15 minutes, totaling 27 minutes; the distance is 5+7=12 kilometers. Fares receivable are 6×2+3×1=15 yuan, of which 10 yuan is electronic and 5 yuan cash receivable; actual receipts total 10+4=14 yuan, so cash is 1 yuan short, and the reason is pending verification rather than automatically judging fault by the passenger or the driver.

Example status: 07:55 on-board warning pending verification → report to the designated reviewer/dispatch → await confirmation, and do not mark ready to depart. 08:27 is only the planned arrival; lacking the material releasing the pending item and the actual departure, the actual arrival cannot be determined, nor can the operation be judged finally completed.
Practice and real authority

All inputs and procedures are fictional paper materials, and the answers only prove that the calculation and records are reviewable, not that the vehicle is airworthy, the person is competent to drive, or the operation is compliant. U.S. bus drivers need a CDL and the applicable P passenger endorsement, issued by the state, verified by vehicle class and state rules; entry-level A/B or initial P, among others, require separate verification of ELDT applicability and exceptions.

In China, drivers engaged in commercial road passenger transport follow Article 9 of the 2026 practice provisions: the corresponding motor vehicle driving license for at least 1 year, age no older than 63, no major or greater at-fault traffic accident within 3 years, mastery of road passenger transport regulations and basic motor vehicle repair and passenger first aid knowledge, and passing an examination to obtain the corresponding practice qualification. 63 is not the age threshold for all motor vehicle driving licenses, and urban bus positions are verified separately under urban rules. Urban buses are verified under Articles 31—32 of the 2024 regulation and Articles 27—28 of the 2017 rules for duty capability, health, no violent crime or drug record, a matching driving license with the driving probationary period completed, no full 12 points in 3 consecutive scoring cycles, and no traffic accident crime, dangerous driving crime, or drink-driving record; training and assessment must be passed before taking up the post, archives must be kept for inspection, and filing with the competent department is made per the rules.
